title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Clerval then put the following letter into my hands. It was from my own Elizabeth:
"My dearest Cousin,

"You have been ill, very ill, and even dear kind Henry's constant letters aren't enough to reassure me. You're forbidden to write or even hold a pen. Yet one word from you, dear Victor, is all we need to calm our fears. I've been expecting that word with every post, and I've managed to stop my uncle from making the long journey to Ingolstadt. I've spared him the difficulties and possible dangers of such a trip, yet how often I've wished I could go myself! I imagined some hired nurse attending your sickbed — someone who could never guess your needs or care for you with the love your poor cousin would. But that's over now. Clerval writes that you're getting better. I eagerly hope you'll confirm this soon in your own handwriting.

"Get well and come home. You'll find a happy, cheerful household and friends who love you dearly. Your father is in good health. He asks only to see you and to know you're well. Not a single worry will cloud his kind face. How pleased you'd be to see how Ernest has grown! He's sixteen now, full of energy and spirit. He wants to be a true Swiss and enter military service abroad. But we can't let him go, at least not until his elder brother returns. My uncle doesn't like the idea of a military career in a distant country. But Ernest never had your powers of concentration. He thinks of study as a hateful burden. He spends his time outdoors, climbing hills or rowing on the lake. I'm afraid he'll become an idler unless we give in and let him pursue the career he's chosen.

"Little has changed besides the children growing up. The blue lake and snow-capped mountains never change. I think our peaceful home and contented hearts are governed by the same timeless laws. My small occupations fill my time and amuse me. I'm rewarded by seeing nothing but happy, kind faces around me. Since you left, only one change has occurred in our household. Do you remember when Justine Moritz came to our family? Probably not, so let me tell you her story briefly. Her mother, Madame Moritz, was a widow with four children. Justine was the third. She had always been her father's favorite, but through some strange perversity, her mother couldn't stand her. After Monsieur Moritz died, her mother treated her terribly. My aunt noticed this, and when Justine was twelve, persuaded her mother to let her live with us. The republican institutions of our country have created simpler, happier manners than those of the great monarchies around us. The differences between social classes are smaller here. The lower classes, being neither so poor nor so despised, have more refined and moral habits. Being a servant in Geneva doesn't mean the same thing as being a servant in France or England. Justine joined our family and learned a servant's duties — a role which, in our fortunate country, doesn't imply ignorance or loss of human dignity.

"You may remember that Justine was a great favorite of yours. I recall you once said that if you were in a bad mood, one look from Justine could fix it, for the same reason the Italian poet Ariosto gives for the beauty of his heroine Angelica — she looked so open-hearted and happy. My aunt grew very fond of her and gave her a better education than she'd originally planned. Justine repaid this kindness fully. She was the most grateful creature in the world. Not that she made speeches about it — I never heard one leave her lips. But you could see in her eyes that she nearly worshipped her protectress. Though she was cheerful and sometimes careless by nature, she paid the closest attention to every gesture my aunt made. She thought my aunt was the model of perfection and tried to imitate her way of speaking and behaving. Even now she often reminds me of her.

"When my dearest aunt died, everyone was too consumed by their own grief to notice poor Justine, who had nursed her through her final illness with the most devoted care. Poor Justine was very ill herself. But other trials awaited her.

"One by one, her brothers and sister died. Apart from the daughter she had neglected, her mother was left childless. The woman's conscience troubled her. She began to think these deaths were heaven's punishment for her favoritism. She was a Roman Catholic, and I believe her confessor encouraged this idea. So, a few months after you left for Ingolstadt, Justine's repentant mother called her home. Poor girl! She wept when she left our house. She was much changed since my aunt's death. Grief had softened her and given her a quiet sweetness that replaced her former liveliness. Living with her mother didn't restore her spirits. The poor woman swung back and forth in her repentance — sometimes begging Justine to forgive her cruelty, but more often accusing her of causing her siblings' deaths. Her constant fretting eventually threw Madame Moritz into a decline, which at first made her even more irritable. But she is now at peace forever. She died when the cold weather first came, at the start of this past winter. Justine has just returned to us. I assure you I love her dearly. She's very clever, gentle, and extremely pretty. As I mentioned, her manner and expression constantly remind me of my dear aunt.

"I must also say a few words about little darling William. I wish you could see him! He's very tall for his age, with sweet laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes, and curly hair. When he smiles, two little dimples appear on each rosy, healthy cheek. He already has one or two little _wives_, but his favorite is Louisa Biron, a pretty little girl of five.

"Now, dear Victor, I'm sure you want some gossip about the good people of Geneva. The pretty Miss Mansfield has already received congratulations on her upcoming marriage to a young Englishman, John Melbourne, Esq. Her ugly sister, Manon, married Monsieur Duvillard, the rich banker, last autumn. Your favorite schoolmate, Louis Manoir, has suffered several misfortunes since Clerval left Geneva. But he's recovered his spirits and is reportedly about to marry a lively, pretty Frenchwoman, Madame Tavernier. She's a widow, much older than Manoir, but she's greatly admired and a favorite with everyone.

"Writing this has put me in better spirits, dear cousin. But my anxiety returns as I finish. Write, dearest Victor — one line, one word would be a blessing to us. Ten thousand thanks to Henry for his kindness, his love, and his many letters. We're sincerely grateful. Farewell, my cousin! Take care of yourself, and I beg you — write!
"Elizabeth Lavenza.
"Geneva, March 18th, 17—."

"Dear, dear Elizabeth!" I exclaimed when I'd finished her letter. "I'll write immediately and relieve their anxiety." I wrote, and the effort greatly tired me. But my recovery had begun and continued steadily. Within another two weeks I was able to leave my room.

One of my first duties after recovering was to introduce Clerval to the university professors. This put me through a kind of ordeal ill-suited to the wounds my mind had suffered. Ever since that fatal night — the end of my labors and the beginning of my misfortunes — I'd developed a violent hatred for even the name of natural philosophy. Even when I was otherwise fully recovered, merely seeing a chemical instrument would bring back all the agony of my nervous symptoms. Henry recognized this and removed all my equipment from sight. He'd also moved me to a different room, sensing my hatred for the one that had been my laboratory. But these precautions were useless when I visited the professors. Professor Waldman tortured me when he praised, with kindness and warmth, the astonishing progress I'd made in science. He soon noticed my discomfort but didn't guess the real cause. Attributing my reaction to modesty, he changed the subject from my achievements to the science itself, clearly hoping to draw me out. What could I do? He meant to be kind, and he was tormenting me. I felt as if he were carefully placing before me, one by one, the instruments that would later be used to kill me slowly. I squirmed under his words but didn't dare show my pain. Clerval, whose sharp eyes always read others' feelings, steered the conversation away by pleading complete ignorance of the subject, and the talk turned to more general matters. I silently thanked him from the depths of my heart. I could clearly see his surprise, but he never tried to extract my secret. Though I loved him with boundless affection and reverence, I could never bring myself to confide in him about the event that haunted my memory. I feared that telling someone else would only imprint it more deeply on my mind.

Professor Krempe was less tactful. In my almost unbearably sensitive state, his blunt, harsh compliments caused me even more pain than Professor Waldman's kind praise. "Damn the fellow!" he cried. "Monsieur Clerval, I assure you he's surpassed us all. Yes, stare if you like, but it's true. A young man who just a few years ago believed in Cornelius Agrippa as firmly as the gospel has now put himself at the head of the university. If we don't pull him down soon, we'll all be put to shame. Ah, yes," he continued, noticing the suffering in my face, "Monsieur Frankenstein is modest. An excellent quality in a young man. Young men should be modest, Monsieur Clerval. I was modest myself once, but that wears off quickly."
Professor Krempe had now launched into praising himself, which thankfully steered the conversation away from a subject that was agony for me.

Clerval had never shared my interest in natural science. His scholarly pursuits were completely different from mine. He'd come to the university to master the Oriental languages, which would help him realize his life plan. Determined to pursue a distinguished career, he'd turned his gaze toward the East as a field for his ambitious spirit. Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit occupied his attention. I was easily persuaded to join him in these studies. Idleness had always been unbearable to me. Now that I wanted to escape my own thoughts and hated my old studies, I found great relief in being a fellow student with my friend. The works of the Orientalists gave me not just learning but consolation. I didn't try to master the languages critically, as Henry did, since I only intended them as temporary distraction. I read simply for meaning, and they amply rewarded my efforts. Their melancholy is soothing and their joy uplifting to a degree I'd never experienced in any other literature. When you read their writings, life seems to consist of a warm sun and a garden of roses — the smiles and frowns of a beautiful adversary, and the fire consuming your own heart. How different from the manly, heroic poetry of Greece and Rome!

Summer passed in these activities. My return to Geneva was planned for late autumn. But several delays pushed it back. Winter came, the roads became impassable, and my journey was postponed until spring. I felt this delay keenly, for I longed to see my hometown and my beloved friends. I'd only stayed so long because I was reluctant to leave Clerval in a strange place before he'd made acquaintances. The winter passed cheerfully, though. And when spring finally came — uncommonly late — its beauty made up for the wait.

May had already begun. I was expecting the letter that would set my departure date when Henry proposed a walking tour of the countryside around Ingolstadt, so I could say a personal farewell to the area I'd lived in so long. I happily agreed. I was fond of exercise, and Clerval had always been my favorite companion on such outings in our native country.

We spent two weeks on this ramble. My health and spirits had long since recovered, and they gained extra strength from the fresh air, the natural sights along our way, and my friend's conversation. Study had previously cut me off from other people and made me unsociable. But Clerval drew out the better feelings in my heart. He taught me again to love nature's beauty and children's cheerful faces. Excellent friend! How genuinely you loved me and tried to lift my mind to the level of your own. A selfish obsession had cramped and narrowed me until your gentleness and warmth opened my senses again. I became the same happy person who, a few years earlier, loved and was loved by all, with no sorrow or care. When I was happy, nature could give me the most delightful feelings. A clear sky and green fields filled me with bliss. This season was truly divine — spring flowers blooming in the hedges, summer buds already forming. I was free of the thoughts that had weighed on me the previous year despite my efforts to shake them off.

Henry rejoiced in my cheerfulness and shared my feelings wholeheartedly. He did everything he could to amuse me, while also expressing the feelings that filled his own soul. His mind was remarkably alive on these occasions. His conversation sparkled with imagination. Often, imitating the Persian and Arabic writers, he invented tales of wonderful fantasy and passion. Other times he recited my favorite poems or drew me into debates, which he conducted with great cleverness.

We returned to the university on a Sunday afternoon. Peasants were dancing. Everyone we met seemed happy and cheerful. My own spirits were high. I bounded along with feelings of unbounded joy and delight.
